books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889
Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)
H. Leh and Company newspaper advertisement, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890
United States Census Bureau, urban population figures, 1870-1890
Scene at Coney Island chromolithograph trade card, Lindner, Eddy and Clauss, ca. 1885-1896
Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Women and Economics (1898)

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the growth of the middle class changed American society in the period 1865–1898.

documents.title: Carnegie on the Administration of Wealth
documents.source: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A steel maker writing for a magazine read by the educated middle class, arguing that the rich should give during their lives.
documents.text:
“There are but three modes in which surplus wealth can be disposed of. It can be left to the families of the decedents; or it can be bequeathed for public purposes; or, finally, it can be administered during their lives by its possessors....

This policy would work powerfully to induce the rich man to attend to the administration of wealth during his life, which is the end that society should always have in view, as being that by far most fruitful for the people.”

documents.title: Riis on the Tenements
documents.source: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (Charles Scribner's Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Danish immigrant and police reporter writing to show comfortable readers the slum conditions they ignored.
documents.text: “Of one thing New York made sure at that early stage of the inquiry: the boundary line of the Other Half lies through the tenements. ... To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them.”

documents.title: Department-Store Advertisement
documents.source: Newspaper advertisement for H. Leh and Company, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A store's own advertisement, made to bring shoppers in; it shows what the store wanted customers to see.

documents.title: The Office Typewriter
documents.source: Remington Standard typewriter, 1890. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: An engraving of the machine that created typing jobs; it shows the tool, not the worker who used it.

documents.title: The Urban Share of the Population Grows
documents.source: United States Census Bureau, urban population as a percentage of total population (places of 2,500 or more).
documents.sourcing: Census figures showing the cities growing faster than the country as a whole through the period.
documents.text:
| Year | Share of Americans living in urban places |
| 1870 | 25.7% |
| 1880 | 28.2% |
| 1890 | 35.1% |

documents.title: A Day at Coney Island
documents.source: Chromolithograph trade card, “Scene at Coney Island,” Lindner, Eddy and Clauss, New York, ca. 1885-1896. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A trade card made to sell children's clothing; its cheerful beach scene is the leisure the firm wanted buyers to picture.

documents.title: Gilman on Women's Work
documents.source: Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Women and Economics (1898), Chapters 8 and 10. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A reform writer arguing that women's lives should reach beyond the home, at a time when women were entering offices and schools.
documents.text:
“There is no female mind. The brain is not an organ of sex. As well speak of a female liver.”

“Only as we live, think, feel, and work outside the home, do we become humanly developed, civilized, socialized.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the growth of the middle class changed American society between 1865 and 1898, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization creating corporations and cities, the growth of urban population, or the older middle class of the early nineteenth century.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the middle class and American society.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as Hull House (1889), the expansion of public high schools from 100 in 1860 to about 6,000 by 1900, or electric streetcars and streetcar suburbs.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, showing that the middle class both benefited from industrialization and criticized its harms, or explaining why the same growth produced different results for men and women, or for the middle class and the poor.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 the growth of the middle class changed American society a great deal, creating new work, new shopping, new suburbs, and new reform energy, though the change reached the cities far more than the countryside and left the poor behind.
Context: Industrialization built giant corporations and crowded cities, while the urban share of the population rose from about a quarter in 1870 to over a third in 1890, and the old middle class of small shopkeepers and farmers gave way to salaried office workers.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 7 show the ideas that came with the new class, Carnegie's duty of giving and Gilman's claim for women's work outside the home.
Evidence continued: Documents 3 and 4 show its daily life, advertised prices and brand names in a department-store ad and the typewriter that filled offices with women typists. Document 5 measures the city growth behind it all, and Document 6 shows its leisure, a crowded commercial beach. Document 2 shows its other side, the tenements the middle class looked down on and then tried to reform.
Beyond the documents: Hull House opened in Chicago in 1889, public high schools grew from 100 in 1860 to about 6,000 by 1900, and electric streetcars let families buy homes in early suburbs.
Sourcing: Carnegie writes as a rich man defending his own class to magazine readers, while Riis writes as a reporter accusing comfortable readers of not caring; the Leh ad and the Coney Island card were both made to sell, so they show the shopping and leisure firms wanted buyers to picture.
Complexity: The change was real but uneven. The middle class bought the new economy's goods and took its salaries, yet its reformers attacked the slums and the abuses the same economy produced, so one class both carried industrialization forward and tried to fix it.
